Case studies/Lapland cattle
Finland

Lapland cattle.

Genetic heritage and Arctic resilience

Connecting the cultural value of Northern Finncattle with research into adaptation, resilience and genetic conservation.

Northern Finncattle, known in Finnish as Lapin Lehmä, have long been part of the livelihoods of Finnish Lapland. After the breed was reduced almost to extinction, conservation efforts helped restore its population.

This case combines anthropology and genetics to investigate relationships between local accounts of resilience, cultural understandings of sustainability and the biological characteristics of the breed.

The Luke animal genomics team studies whole genomes, gene expression and regulatory mechanisms associated with environmental adaptation. Its wider comparative work includes other northern cattle breeds, reindeer and horses, connecting local conservation questions to research across northern environments.

The September 2026 Luke update reports that Northern Finncattle narrowly escaped extinction in the 1980s and records approximately 850 breeding cows. The principal conservation herd is maintained at the educational farm of Vocational College Lappia in Tervola, Finnish Lapland. Embryos and bull semen are also stored in the national animal genetic resources cryobank.

The project overview describes farmers exploring production based on milk, meat and other products. It highlights the value placed on the breed’s hardiness, modest feeding requirements, disease resilience and high-fat milk in local farming environments.

How we work

Anthropological fieldwork, whole-genome sequencing, transcriptomics, microRNA profiling and comparative bioinformatics.

Source material: Luke website update · September 2026.
